Clinical Trial Effectiveness of R21/Matrix-M
Setting	Efficacy	Duration	Key Details
Seasonal transmission areas	75% efficacy	12 months after 3-dose series	High transmission limited to 4–5 months per year
Year-round (age-based schedule)	66-68% efficacy	12 months after 3-dose series	Regions with perennial malaria presence
Booster dose	Maintained efficacy	12 months after 4th dose	Administered 1 year after 3rd dose

Trial Design and Population

The R21/Matrix-M vaccine demonstrated high effectiveness in clinical trials across sub-Saharan Africa. The primary Phase 3 efficacy trial enrolled 4,800 children aged 5–36 months across multiple sites in four African countries. 
 [1]

The vaccine reduced symptomatic malaria cases by 75% in areas with highly seasonal transmission when administered just before the high transmission season. 
 [2]
 In regions where malaria is present throughout the year, the vaccine showed 66-68% efficacy during the 12 months following the first three doses when given on an age-based vaccination schedule. 
 [2]

A fourth booster dose given one year after the third dose maintained efficacy in both seasonal and perennial transmission settings. 
 [2]

Safety Profile

The R21/Matrix-M vaccine was well tolerated in clinical trials. The most common adverse events were fever (47%) and injection site pain (19%). 
 [1]
 These are typical, mild side effects commonly observed with other vaccines. The vaccine was shown to be safe in clinical trials, with WHO noting that as with other new vaccines, ongoing safety monitoring will continue. 
 [2]

Public Health Significance

The WHO recommended R21/Matrix-M in October 2023, making it the second malaria vaccine approved by the organization (following RTS,S/AS01). 
 [2]
 Mathematical modelling indicates the vaccine is expected to have high public health impact across a wide range of malaria transmission settings, including low transmission areas. 
 [2]
 At a cost of $2–$4 per dose, the vaccine demonstrates cost-effectiveness comparable to other recommended malaria interventions and childhood vaccines. 
 [2]
